section.title: Blessed Is the Man Who Fears the Lord
section.sectionRationale: The twin acrostic to Psalm 111, this psalm describes the flourishing, generous, unshaken life that results when a person fears the great God the previous psalm celebrates, closing the pair by contrasting the righteous with the wicked.
section.thesis: The one who fears the LORD and delights in His commands receives an unshaken, generous, and enduring life, a stability that flows not from circumstance but from a heart anchored in God while the schemes of the wicked come to nothing.
section.frameNote: Three movements mirroring the acrostic structure: the foundation of blessing in fearing the LORD, with legacy and provision that follow, verses 1-4; steadfast stability and fearless confidence in the LORD amid bad news, verses 5-9; and the closing contrast with the wicked, whose desires perish, verse 10.

units.label: Blessed is the man who fears the LORD

verses.text: Hallelujah! Blessed is the man who fears the LORD, who greatly delights in His commandments.
His descendants will be mighty in the land; the generation of the upright will be blessed.
Wealth and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures forever.
Light dawns in the darkness for the upright, for the gracious, compassionate, and righteous.
It is well with the man who is generous and lends freely, whose affairs are guided by justice.
Surely he will never be {{mot|shaken}}; the righteous man will be remembered forever.
He does not fear bad news; his heart is steadfast, trusting in the LORD.
His heart is assured; he does not fear, until he looks in triumph on his foes.
He has scattered abroad his {{tsedaqah|gifts}} to the poor; his righteousness endures forever; his horn will be lifted high in honor.
The wicked man will see and be grieved; he will gnash his teeth and waste away; the desires of the wicked will perish.

mot.gloss: To slip, totter, be shaken loose. The righteous person built on the fear of the LORD is pictured as immovable, not because circumstances never shake, but because the foundation beneath him holds firm.

tsedaqah.gloss: Righteousness, but here specifically expressed as generous giving to the poor. Paul quotes this exact verse, 2 Corinthians 9:9, to root Christian generosity in the same enduring righteousness this psalm describes.

basic.context: The twin of Psalm 111, this acrostic hymn moves from praising the great God to describing the flourishing, generous, and unshaken life of the one who fears Him, closing with a brief but sharp contrast to the wicked, whose hopes come to nothing.
basic.hermeneutics: The blessings described, legacy, wealth, stability, are not a formula guaranteeing prosperity to anyone who merely performs religious duties, but a portrait of the settled confidence and generous character that genuinely flows from a heart anchored in reverent trust of the LORD.
basic.originalLanguages: The righteous man will never be mot, shaken or toppled, verse 6, because his heart, verse 7, is fixed on the LORD rather than on circumstance. His giving is described as tsedaqah, righteousness expressed in generosity, verse 9, a verse Paul later applies directly to Christian giving, 2 Corinthians 9:9.
basic.typology: The steadfast, fearless, generous man of this psalm anticipates Christ, who delighted perfectly in His Father's commandments, John 8:29, brought light into darkness, John 1:4-5, gave generously to the poor, and whose righteousness endures forever without any need of renewal.
basic.christ: Jesus embodies this psalm's portrait perfectly, delighting in His Father's will, John 8:29, and Paul explicitly quotes verse 9, He has scattered abroad his gifts to the poor, his righteousness endures forever, 2 Corinthians 9:9, applying this psalm's generosity to the pattern of Christ, who though rich became poor so that His people might become rich, 2 Corinthians 8:9.
basic.god: God is the one whose commandments are worth delighting in, whose provision undergirds true wealth and legacy, and who is the steady object of trust that keeps the righteous heart unshaken even when bad news arrives.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Corinthians 9:9 quotes verse 9 directly, applying its language of generous, enduring righteousness to Christian giving. Proverbs 9:10 echoes verse 1's foundation, the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. Psalm 1 provides a similar contrast between the flourishing righteous and the perishing wicked.
basic.oneStory: The unshaken, generous life described here flows entirely from fearing and delighting in the LORD, a portrait perfectly fulfilled in Christ, whose own righteousness endures forever and whose generosity toward the poor, quoted directly by Paul, becomes the pattern and the power for every believer's steadfast, giving life.

context.literary:
Psalm 112 is built to be read in the shadow of Psalm 111. It is an acrostic of the same length and the same lineation, twenty-two short lines, with the same rhythm of two lines to a verse and three lines in each of the last two. More than that, whole phrases are carried across. The statement in Psalm 111:3 that 'His righteousness endures forever' becomes 'his righteousness endures forever' here in verses 3 and 9. The pair 'gracious and compassionate' is used of God in Psalm 111:4, and it appears again in verse 4 of this psalm, where it fits the upright person. Psalm 111:8 says that God's precepts are 'upheld,' and Psalm 112:8 says that the believer's heart is 'upheld.' The poet is plainly saying that the person who fears the LORD is shaped by the God who is praised in the first psalm.

The structure moves from the person to the person's world and then to the person's inner life. Verses 1 to 3 give the blessing in the family and the household. Verses 4 to 6 turn to the character that produces it: light, grace, generosity and justice, ending with the promise of memory. Verses 7 to 9 describe the heart under pressure, where the person does not fear and does not shake. Verse 10 is a single sharp verse about the wicked, and it works as a frame that shows what the other nine verses were set against.

The word 'fear' is the thread. The psalm begins with the man who 'fears the LORD,' verse 1, and in verses 7 and 8 the same man 'does not fear' bad news and 'does not fear' at all. The one fear drives out the others, and the two uses of the same Hebrew root, yare, are meant to be heard together.
context.historical:
The first hearers lived under a covenant that promised blessing for obedience, and this psalm would have sounded to them like a picture of Deuteronomy 28:1-6 turned into a life. The blessings of descendants, land, household and honour are all there. But the psalm is not only about reward, and Israel's wisdom writers knew how complicated the matter was. Job 21:7-9 asks why the wicked prosper, and Psalm 73:3-5 shows a believer almost losing his footing as he envied them. A first hearer would not have treated verse 3 as a guarantee; the same community that sang this psalm also sang those.

The generosity at the centre of the psalm has roots in the law. Deuteronomy 15:7-11 forbids a hard heart and a shut hand toward a poor neighbour and commands a lender to 'open wide your hand,' and it warns against lending grudgingly because the year of release was near. Psalm 15:5 also counts lending without interest among the marks of the person who 'will never be shaken,' the same promise that the psalm gives in verse 6. In an agricultural society where a poor harvest could force a family into debt, a willingness to lend freely was a mark of true righteousness.

The picture of 'bad news' in verse 7 would have had a concrete meaning in a world of raids, famine and war, where reports came by messenger and could change a life in a day. The 'horn' lifted high in verse 9 was an image of strength and honour, used of an anointed king in 1 Samuel 2:10. The closing picture of the wicked who gnash their teeth belongs to the same world as Psalm 37:12, where the wicked 'gnash their teeth' at the righteous.
context.canonical:
Psalm 112 belongs to a family of psalms and proverbs that describe the blessed life, beginning with Psalm 1. There the blessed person delights in the law and 'prospers in all he does,' and the wicked 'will perish,' Psalm 1:2-6. Psalm 112 begins in the same way, 'Blessed is the man,' and ends with the same verb, 'the desires of the wicked will perish.' The two psalms say the same thing from different ends of the Psalter. Proverbs offers many of the same ideas on generosity, such as 'A generous soul will prosper,' Proverbs 11:25, and 'Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD,' Proverbs 19:17.

The strongest link in the New Testament is in 2 Corinthians 9. Paul urges the Corinthians to give generously to the poor in Jerusalem, and he cites verse 9 as the voice of Scripture: 'He has scattered abroad His gifts to the poor; His righteousness endures forever,' 2 Corinthians 9:9. He then goes on to speak of God, who 'supplies seed to the sower,' and who will 'increase the harvest of your righteousness,' 2 Corinthians 9:10. Paul takes a psalm about a godly person and shows that the generosity comes from the grace of God.

Jesus echoes the psalm's themes in the Sermon on the Mount. His call to give in secret and to store up treasure in heaven, Matthew 6:1-4 and 6:19-21, deals with the same impulse, and His promise that the one who builds on the rock will not fall, Matthew 7:24-25, is close to the 'never be shaken' of verse 6. In Luke 6:35 He tells His followers to lend 'expecting nothing in return,' which carries the psalm's generous lending into the way of the kingdom.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet is writing a companion to a hymn, and his aim is to answer a question the first psalm raises. If God is as the congregation has just said, gracious, compassionate, righteous and faithful, what kind of person does a God like that produce? The answer is a portrait, and it is drawn to be admired and then copied. The first hearers were meant to see in it a person they would want to be.

The portrait is deliberately balanced. The person delights in God's commandments, verse 1, and also gives to the poor, verse 9, so that devotion and generosity are held together and neither is allowed to stand alone. He is confident but not careless, because his confidence is rooted in trust in the LORD, verse 7, and he is generous but not foolish, because his affairs are 'guided by justice,' verse 5. The poet means to correct a division that people often make, between private piety and public conduct.

He also means to give courage. The listeners lived in a world where bad news could arrive at any time, and the psalm tells them that fear of the LORD is the thing that frees them from fear of everything else. The last verse is a reminder that the wicked have no such security, and that their plans will come to nothing. A first hearer would have left the assembly steadier and more ready to be open-handed.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes a person and does not issue commands, so the way to apply it is to ask what kind of person it describes and whether the reader wants to be that person. The description of wealth and honour in verses 2 and 3 should be read as the poet's picture of a typical outcome under God's care and not as a promise that every believer will be rich. The same Scriptures that speak of blessing also record righteous people who suffered, as Ecclesiastes 8:14 observes, so the pattern is real but not mechanical.

What carries forward without difficulty is the character: delight in God's commandments, grace toward others, honest dealing, open-handed lending, a settled heart under bad news. These are the qualities the New Testament commends. Paul does not say the Corinthians will be rich if they give; he says that God will supply and multiply, 2 Corinthians 9:10-11, and he gives the purpose as thanksgiving to God. The psalm should therefore not be turned into a formula for gain. It is better read as a description of the life that results when a person's fear is settled on God, with the blessings left in His hands.

debates.question: Does the psalm promise material prosperity to everyone who fears the LORD?

views.label: It describes a general pattern, not a guarantee
views.case: Proverbs, Job and Ecclesiastes all hold that the righteous often do well but not always. Job 21:7-9 and Psalm 73:3-5 face the opposite case squarely. On this reading, the wealth and descendants of verses 2 and 3 are the usual outcome of a life lived under God's moral order, and the psalm does not say that each person will get each blessing.

views.label: It speaks of true riches and a lasting legacy
views.case: Verse 3 sets 'wealth and riches' beside 'his righteousness endures forever,' so what lasts is righteousness and not the house. The man is remembered forever, verse 6, which is a different kind of wealth. Jesus' words about treasure in heaven, Matthew 6:20, show that the greater riches are those that do not wear out.

views.label: It is a blessing pronounced for the whole covenant community
views.case: Some read the psalm as a statement about Israel's life as a people. The promise of descendants who are mighty in the land fits a covenant community whose members' blessing is shared, as in Deuteronomy 28:1-6.

debates.bearing: The psalm should be held as a wise observation about how God's world usually works, kept next to the harder books of the Bible. It tells the believer what to aim at, and it does not entitle anyone to demand a particular outcome.

debates.question: In verse 4, who is 'gracious, compassionate, and righteous'?

views.label: The upright person
views.case: The BSB takes the three words as a description of the upright, and the same psalm describes the godly person's generosity in verse 5, which fits grace and compassion. Light dawns for people who are like that, as in Isaiah 58:10, where giving to the hungry brings light in the darkness.

views.label: God Himself
views.case: The three Hebrew adjectives are singular and the verse does not name who they describe, and 'gracious and compassionate' are the very words used of the LORD in Psalm 111:4, with righteousness His in Psalm 111:3. On this reading God is the light who dawns for the upright, as in Psalm 27:1 and Psalm 97:11. The believer's own light is thus a gift, not an achievement.

debates.bearing: The psalm may intend both. The upright person is gracious because God is gracious, and the line may be doing double duty on purpose, so that the believer's light is a reflection of the God he fears.

study.originalLanguages:
The psalm begins with the man 'who fears the LORD,' using the root yare, and then, in verses 7 and 8, says that he 'does not fear' bad news and 'does not fear' at all, using the same root in a negative form. The opening verse also says that he 'greatly delights' in the commandments, from the verb chaphets. The same root appears in Psalm 111:2, where the works of God are studied by 'all who delight in them.' The person who delights in God's works also delights in His commands.

The relation to Psalm 111 goes further in verse 4. The words 'gracious, compassionate, and righteous' are the same words that Psalm 111:3 and 4 use of God. The effect is that the believer takes on God's own character: what is said of the LORD in the hymn is said of the one who fears Him in the sequel. There is a similar echo in verse 5, where the person is 'generous,' using a participle from the root that gives 'gracious,' chanan, so the believer's generosity is called by the same name as God's grace.

In verse 5 the person 'lends freely,' and the word is a participle of lavah, to lend. The same root is used in Proverbs 19:17 of lending to the LORD, and in Deuteronomy 28:12 of the blessing that Israel will lend to many nations and not borrow. In verse 6 the righteous man will be remembered 'forever,' and the Hebrew word for remembrance is zekher, the same word used in Psalm 111:4 of God's memorial of His wonders. God makes a memorial of His works, and He makes a memorial of the person who trusts Him.

Verse 7 describes a heart that is nakhon, firm or established, and verse 8 says the heart is samukh, supported or propped up. Psalm 111:8 says that God's precepts are semukhim, upheld, so the heart of the believer is held up by the same support that holds up the commands. Verse 7 also says the person is batuach, trusting, and this is the root that stands behind the quiet confidence found in many of the psalms.

The word in verse 9 that the BSB renders as 'scattered abroad' is pizzar, a verb that carries the idea of strewing or dispersing, as seed is scattered. The generosity is spread wide and is not measured out. The word 'righteousness,' tsedaqah, stands in the second line, and in the BSB of the first line it appears as 'gifts.' In later Hebrew the word came to mean charitable giving, and Jesus' teaching on giving to the needy in Matthew 6:1-2 comes under the heading of 'righteous acts.' The psalm sees giving as a form of doing right.

The final line of verse 9, 'his horn will be lifted high,' uses the word qeren, horn, for strength and dignity, as in Hannah's prayer, 1 Samuel 2:1 and 2:10. The last verse says that the desire of the wicked will 'perish,' from the verb abad, the same verb that ends Psalm 1:6, 'the way of the wicked will perish.'

typology.type: The man who delights in the commandments, verse 1
typology.fulfillment: The psalm sets a blessed person who loves God's commands, and the New Testament shows that the pattern is truly fulfilled in only one man. Jesus said, 'I always do what pleases Him,' John 8:29, and Isaiah promised of the Branch that 'He will delight in the fear of the LORD,' Isaiah 11:3. In Christ the delight is perfect and unbroken. The escalation is that He is not only the model but the one who gives His people a new heart to love what He loved. The type falls short in that every other godly person in the Old Testament stumbled, and this portrait is only ever partly seen in them.

typology.type: Light dawning in the darkness, verse 4
typology.fulfillment: The light that dawns on the upright is a picture that the Gospels fill in. John says of Jesus, 'In Him was life, and that life was the light of men,' and that the light 'shines in the darkness,' John 1:4-5. Jesus says, 'I am the light of the world,' and promises that His followers will 'have the light of life,' John 8:12. The correspondence is a light that comes from God for those in need. The escalation is that the light is a Person and He is also the source of the believer's own light, as in Matthew 5:14-16. The type falls short because the psalm's light is a dawn within history, while Christ's is the light of the age to come.

typology.type: The scattered gifts to the poor, verse 9
typology.fulfillment: The generosity described in the psalm is a pale picture of the generosity of Christ. Paul uses the psalm to prompt giving and then points to its true source: 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich,' 2 Corinthians 8:9. The man of the psalm gives from what he has; Christ gives up what He had. The pattern is fulfilled in the incarnation and the cross, and believers who give are following in His steps. The type falls short because the psalm's giver gives wealth, while Christ gave Himself.

typology.type: The heart that is never shaken, verses 6 to 8
typology.fulfillment: The settled heart of the psalm is seen in its fullness in Jesus, who slept in the storm and who said to His disciples, 'Do not let your hearts be troubled,' John 14:1, and 'do not be afraid,' John 14:27. At Gethsemane He felt the full weight of fear and yet submitted, so His steadiness was not an absence of feeling, Matthew 26:39. Paul draws the same kind of confidence for those in Christ, who are 'more than conquerors,' Romans 8:35-39. The type falls short in that the psalm's person is secure by his own trust, while the believer's security rests on Christ's love that cannot be broken.

study.christ:
Psalm 112 leads to Christ as a portrait that no one but He completely fills. The person it describes delights in God's commandments, gives freely, stands firm against bad news, and has a righteousness that endures forever. Each of these is a claim that the Gospels make for Jesus, and each is also a calling He places on His people.

The delight in God's will is found in His own words. 'I always do what pleases Him,' He says of the Father, John 8:29, and Isaiah looked ahead to a Branch on whom the Spirit would rest and who 'will delight in the fear of the LORD,' Isaiah 11:2-3. The psalm opens with 'blessed is the man who fears the LORD' and Jesus opens His great sermon with a run of blessings, Matthew 5:3-10, that describe the same kind of person, the poor in spirit, the merciful, the pure in heart.

The light dawning in the darkness is His. He says, 'I am the light of the world,' John 8:12, and John writes that His light shines in the darkness and the darkness has not overcome it, John 1:4-5. When Matthew describes the beginning of Jesus' ministry, he shows light dawning on people who sat in darkness. The line of the psalm that God is gracious, compassionate and righteous is fulfilled in the person of the one who is 'full of grace and truth,' John 1:14.

The generosity of verse 9 is the closest link, because Paul himself makes it. He quotes the verse to urge the Corinthians to give and then, a chapter earlier, points to the grace of the Lord Jesus, 'that though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor,' 2 Corinthians 8:9. The scattered gifts of the psalm are surpassed by the one who gave Himself. His righteousness endures forever, because it is the righteousness that He gives to His people, so that those who have none may stand before God, 1 Corinthians 1:30.

The steady heart is also His. In a boat on a storm-tossed lake He slept, Mark 4:38, and in Gethsemane He faced the worst news of all and prayed, 'Yet not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39. The writer of Hebrews tells us to fix our eyes on Jesus, who 'endured the cross, scorning its shame,' and who sat down at God's right hand, Hebrews 12:2. The horn lifted high in honour is fulfilled in the exaltation of the one who was humbled. Philippians 2:9 says that God 'exalted Him to the highest place.'

A caution is needed. Psalm 112 is not a prediction of Jesus, and the New Testament does not cite it of Him directly. It is a portrait of the godly person that Jesus embodies and makes possible. That is why Paul can apply it to ordinary Christians in Corinth: those who are in Christ share in the character that He perfectly displays.
study.god:
The psalm shows God mostly from the side, through the person who fears Him, and it teaches a good deal about Him in that way. The first lesson is that God is the source of what is good in His people. The words used of the godly person in this psalm, gracious, compassionate and righteous, are used of God in the psalm before it. The one who fears the LORD becomes like Him, and that tells us that God's character is meant to be shared and not only admired.

He is a God who blesses obedience. The first verse gives a blessing to the person who fears Him and delights in His commandments, and the following verses speak of descendants, honour and a lasting name. This is a God who is generous, and who attaches His gifts to a life of trust and not to cleverness or birth. But the psalm does not make Him a vending machine. The blessings are described as the outcome of a life shaped by fear of the LORD, and the psalm leaves the details in His hands.

He is a God who cares for the poor. The psalm never says this directly, but it assumes it. A person who fears the LORD gives to the poor, and the generosity is called righteousness, verse 9. This fits the God of the law, who commanded that a hand be opened to the needy, Deuteronomy 15:7-11, and who says that kindness to the poor is a loan to Himself, Proverbs 19:17. God is on the side of those who are in need, and He wants His people to be on their side too.

He is a God who steadies. The heart that is 'steadfast, trusting in the LORD' does not fear bad news, verse 7. The psalm does not tell us that no bad news will come, but that it will not shake the person who trusts Him. The security is in the object of trust and not in the circumstances. The same teaching appears in Psalm 46:1-2, where God is a refuge and strength and so 'we will not fear,' and in Psalm 62:2, where God is the rock and so 'I will never be shaken.'

He is a God who judges. The last verse is short and stark. The wicked will see the blessing of the righteous and be grieved, and their desires will perish. This is not cruelty but justice: what is set against God's way will not last. The psalm's God is neither indifferent to evil nor quick to be moved by the complaint of the wicked.

For worship, the psalm teaches that praise and character belong together. The hymn before it praises God for being gracious, and this one shows what that looks like in a human life. To worship such a God is to become, over time, a little like Him, open-handed, steady and just, and to trust Him with the outcome.

crossReferences.note: The twin psalm. Several of its lines are reused here, 'His righteousness endures forever,' 'gracious and compassionate,' and 'upheld.' The two psalms present God and the person who fears Him as a matched pair.

The model of the blessed person who delights in God's law and prospers, in contrast with the wicked who perish. Psalm 112 begins with the same blessing and ends with the same verb, so the two psalms frame the Psalter's picture of the righteous.

Paul quotes verse 9 to urge generous giving, and then says that God supplies the seed and increases the harvest of righteousness. The psalm's generosity is shown to flow from God's grace and to end in thanksgiving to Him.
The law requires a hand open to the poor, and warns against giving grudgingly. The psalm's picture of the person who lends freely and scatters gifts is a picture of this command kept from the heart.
A generous soul will prosper and the one who refreshes others will be refreshed. This is the wisdom background to the promise that the generous person will be remembered and honoured.

When people share bread with the hungry, their light breaks forth and rises in the darkness. It is a close parallel to verse 4 and shows how generosity and light were joined in the prophets' teaching.
The writer says he has never seen the righteous abandoned, and describes them as generous and quick to lend. It is another acrostic psalm with a similar view of the generous person.

Jesus teaches that giving to the needy should be done in secret, and He files it under 'righteous acts' in verse 1. The psalm, too, counts the scattering of gifts to the poor as righteousness that endures.
Jesus says that He is the light of the world and that His followers will have the light of life. The light dawning in the darkness in verse 4 reaches its fullness in Him.

Though rich, Christ became poor so that others might become rich. Paul sets this just before his quotation of the psalm in the next chapter, and the scattering of gifts is seen in its most complete form in His self-giving.

God is a refuge and strength, so His people will not fear even if the earth is transformed. It expresses the same truth as verses 7 and 8, that the steady heart rests on God and not on the stability of the world.
The person who hears Jesus' words and acts on them is like a man who built on the rock and was not moved by the storm. It matches the promise that the righteous will never be shaken.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture is also the story of what humanity was made to be. Adam was set in a garden to care for it and to reflect the God who made him, and the fall broke that reflection. Psalm 112 is a portrait of a person in whom the image is being restored. He delights in God's word, shares what he has, trusts when circumstances are frightening, and leaves a lasting name. It is a picture of what it looks like to be human again.

That restoration is slow in the Old Testament. The law gave the shape of a generous life, as in Deuteronomy 15, and the wisdom writers praised it, as in Proverbs 11. Israel's own history shows how rarely the picture was seen. The prophets declared that the poor were crushed and that generosity had failed, and they promised a day when God would give a new heart. The picture in the psalm is therefore both a standard and a hope.

In Christ the picture is fulfilled in a person. He delights in His Father's will, John 8:29, He is light in the darkness, John 8:12, and He became poor so that others could become rich, 2 Corinthians 8:9. His righteousness endures forever, and He gives it away, so that people who have no righteousness of their own are made righteous, 1 Corinthians 1:30. Paul takes the psalm and applies it to ordinary Christians, because those who are in Christ are being shaped into His likeness, 2 Corinthians 3:18.

In the church the psalm is lived out as people give, trust and stand firm in a world full of bad news. The early Christians collected money for the poor in Jerusalem, Romans 15:26, as an expression of the generosity the psalm commends. Their steadiness was a witness to those around them.

The new creation answers the last verse and the first. The wicked will no longer trouble the righteous, and the blessing of the first line will be complete. In Revelation 21:4 God wipes away every tear, and 'there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain.' The righteous who 'will be remembered forever' will be those whose names are known to God, and the generous, steady and unshaken life will become the life of everyone in the city where He dwells.

quiz.q: According to verse 1, what marks the blessed man at the foundation of this psalm's portrait?

options.text: He fears the LORD and greatly delights in His commandments.
options.note: This reverent delight, not mere outward performance, is the psalm's starting point.

options.text: He has inherited great wealth from his ancestors.
options.note: The foundation named is fearing the LORD, not inherited wealth, which the psalm mentions only later as a result.

options.text: He has never faced any hardship or bad news.
options.note: The psalm assumes bad news can come, verse 7; the foundation is fearing the LORD despite it.

options.text: He avoids all commandments in favor of personal freedom.
options.note: The verse says the opposite; he greatly delights in God's commandments.

quiz.q: Why, according to verse 7, does the righteous man not fear bad news?

options.text: His heart is steadfast, trusting in the LORD.
options.note: The stability described is rooted in trust, not in the absence of difficult circumstances.

options.text: He never hears any bad news at all.
options.note: The verse assumes bad news can come; his security is in trusting the LORD despite it.

options.text: He has stockpiled enough resources to handle any crisis alone.
options.note: The text credits his steadfast trust in the LORD, not self-reliant stockpiling.

options.text: He is naturally fearless by temperament.
options.note: The confidence described is explicitly rooted in trusting the LORD, not natural temperament.

quiz.q: What does verse 9 say the righteous man has done, and what New Testament passage quotes it directly?

options.text: He has scattered abroad his gifts to the poor, quoted directly in 2 Corinthians 9:9.
options.note: Paul applies this exact verse to the pattern of generous Christian giving.

options.text: He has hoarded his wealth for his own family alone, with no New Testament connection.
options.note: The verse describes generous scattering to the poor, and Paul quotes it directly in 2 Corinthians 9:9.

options.text: He has given only to relatives, quoted in the book of James.
options.note: The giving described is to the poor broadly, and the direct quotation is in 2 Corinthians, not James.

options.text: He has loaned money at high interest, quoted in Romans.
options.note: Verse 5 actually commends fair, generous lending, and the direct quotation of verse 9 is in 2 Corinthians 9:9, not Romans.

quiz.q: How does verse 10 describe the fate of the wicked, in contrast to the righteous?

options.text: They see the righteous man's stability and are grieved, gnashing their teeth as their desires perish.
options.note: This sharp contrast closes the psalm, echoing the pattern of Psalm 1.

options.text: They ultimately receive the same enduring legacy as the righteous.
options.note: The verse says the opposite; their desires perish, unlike the righteous man's enduring legacy.

options.text: They are shown mercy and given a share in the righteous man's wealth.
options.note: The verse describes their grief and the perishing of their desires, not a shared inheritance.

options.text: They remain entirely unaffected by observing the righteous man's life.
options.note: The text says they see and are grieved, indicating they are affected, though negatively, not unaffected.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's portrait of righteousness and generosity connect to Christ?

options.text: Christ, though rich, became poor so His people might become rich, the pattern Paul links directly to this psalm's language of enduring righteousness.
options.note: 2 Corinthians 8:9 and 9:9 together connect this psalm's generosity directly to the gospel pattern of Christ.

options.text: The psalm has no connection to Christ or the New Testament.
options.note: Paul quotes verse 9 directly in 2 Corinthians 9:9, connecting it explicitly to Christian giving rooted in Christ.

options.text: It connects only to Old Testament tithing laws, with no further significance.
options.note: While rooted in Old Testament generosity, the psalm's connection reaches forward specifically to Christ's own self-giving pattern.

options.text: It predicts the exact amount every believer must give financially.
options.note: The psalm describes a character of generosity, not a specific numeric giving formula.

questions: The blessed man delights greatly in God's commandments rather than merely tolerating them. Which of God's commands do you currently find hardest to delight in, and what would help you begin to delight in it?

This psalm says the righteous heart is steadfast and unafraid even when bad news comes, because it trusts the LORD rather than circumstances. What bad news are you currently facing, and where is your heart's true anchor right now?

Verse 9 is quoted by Paul to describe generous Christian giving rooted in Christ's own generosity. Is your own giving currently more like scattering generously or like holding tightly? What would open-handed generosity look like for you this week?

The psalm closes by showing that the wicked's desires ultimately perish, no matter how threatening they appear now. Where do you need to trust that ungodly schemes around you will not have the last word?
Christ became poor so that His people might become rich. How does reflecting on His generosity toward you change the way you view your own resources and possessions this week?

translationNotes.note: Hallelujah transliterates the Hebrew Hallelu Yah, Praise the LORD, opening the psalm just as it closes the acrostic of Psalm 111, forming a deliberate literary bridge between the two twin psalms.
Never be shaken renders mot, a term for slipping or being toppled, describing the righteous man's stability as rooted in trust rather than an absence of hardship.
This verse is quoted verbatim in 2 Corinthians 9:9, where Paul applies its language of enduring righteousness expressed in generosity directly to the pattern of Christian giving.
